explanation: Fires on word-piece tokens in the middle or end of rare, technical or compound words and names (chemical, biomedical and code identifiers, Scandinavian surnames, place names, e.g. 'fructofuran[[ose]]', 'coll[[ench]]yma', 'Chillico[[the]]'). The trigger is a fragment inside a specialized multi-token term, not any particular string. Ordinary function words give weak or no activation.

Fires at clause or sentence boundary points right after a subject or a heading, just before the main content follows: the copula or verb after a demonstrative subject ('That[['s]]', 'These[[ are]]', 'that[[ is]]'), the comma after a speaker attribution ('Graham said[[,]]'), and the punctuation/newline after case captions ('Seventh Circuit[[.]]', 'UNITED STATES OF AMERICA[[,]]'). Weaker on other commas and colons in prose.

Fires on internal or ending sub-word pieces of technical, mostly scientific/medical/chemical terms ('Rietv[[eld]]', 'Thal[[assa]]emia', 'dim[[ethyl]]', 'at[[rophy]]', 'olig[[omers]]') and some code identifiers. The token completes a multi-piece jargon word. Plain-English tokens are weak.

Fires on short function words (mostly 'a', 'at', also 'be', 'my', 'per', 'that', 'is') that come right after a verb, noun or adjective inside an idiom or measurement phrase ('diameter[[ at]] breast height', 'spend[[ a]] few minutes', 'worth[[ a]] pound', 'go about[[ my]] day', 'rebounds[[ per]] game'). Context matters: the word must continue a fixed or semi-fixed phrase in plain prose.

No clear shared feature. It fires on a mix of word pieces in URLs and code ('bit[[.ly]]', 're[[peat]]', '#!/[[bin]]', 'PTR'), technical nouns ('trans[[locations]]', 'pressure'), and ordinary prose words ('a[[ good]] idea', 'a[[ lot]]', 'hint').

Fires on a grab-bag of tokens in formal or technical text: punctuation after abbreviations or before an example ('Nos[[.]]', 'including[[,]]', 'such as[[,]]'), opening parentheses before abbreviations or sample sizes, infinitive 'to' after 'aimed', 'stands', 'link', and broken multibyte characters. There is no single consistent concept.

Fires on the preposition that a preceding word or phrase requires ('with respect[[ to]]', 'prior[[ to]]', 'sequel[[ to]]', 'ahead[[ of]]', 'in front[[ of]]', 'removed[[ from]]', 'lighter[[ than]]', 'same day[[ as]]'). It also fires on string-concatenation operators ('&', '+') in code. The preceding word that sets up the preposition is what drives it.

Fires on the second word of a fixed phrase or collocation, predicted from the word before it: 'take it[[ for]]', 'for[[ granted]]'-type phrases, 'a[[ little]]', 'founded[[ to]]', 'on[[-A]]gain', 'epithelial[[-to]]-mesenchymal', 'post[[-]]conviction', 'way easier'. Mostly prose. The word is the expected continuation of a common multiword expression.

Fires on the 'more particularly / more specifically / in particular' formula and the 'to' or comma after it in patent 'Field of the Invention' openings ('relates to X and, more[[ particularly]],[[ to]] Y'). Other patent boilerplate gives weaker activation.

Fires on the word that completes a common phrase or term: 'take a[[ look]]', 'all that we[[ can]]', 'viewing[[ this]]', 'Niagara Escarp[[ment]]', 'Luteinizing[[ hormone]]', '95%[[ CI]]'. Both everyday idioms and technical compounds count.

Fires on the first token of a line that follows a line break in the middle of a sentence or block (hard-wrapped text, '
[[and]]', '
[[of]]', '
[[IN]]', '
[[at]]'). It also fires on line-initial tokens and indentation in code and lists. Driven by the position right after a newline when the text continues, not by the token's identity.

Mainly fires on the final word piece of medical and disease terms (contr[[actions]], malign[[ancy]], Hem[[ophilia]], COP[[D]], onc[[ology]], short[[ness]] of breath, disorder), with some legal sentencing words ('sentenced[[ to]]', '2[[ years]]'). Also scattered unrelated code tokens.

Fires on structural boundary tokens in code and documents: the start of the line or indentation that closes a block ('    })', '}', 'End Sub', '</head>'), separator lines ('====') and license-header ends, and the first token of a new section or answer ('A:', 'I. BACKGROUND'). Weak in ordinary prose.

Fires on the token that completes a known technical or set multi-token term or idiom: word pieces inside chemical, medical and engineering words (cyclo[[pro]]panation, Emit[[ting]], dehydro[[gen]]ase, pyro[[ly]]sis) and the second word of fixed phrases ('regress to[[ the]] mean', 'Series B[[ round]]', 'pulse[[ pressure]]', 'job[[ offers]]', 'Scopes[[ Trial]]').

Fires on words that mark contrast or a different instance compared with something earlier, especially 'time' in 'this time' (strongest), plus 'different', 'albeit', 'but', 'just', 'much/more' in comparisons, 'another/other'. Needs a contrastive or comparative context.

Fires on words referring to two parties in a relationship or in contact, especially possessive 'their/our' and 'to/have' after a couple or pair is mentioned ('their encounter', 'our sex life', 'met the day before[[ to]]', 'Ike and I have[[ been]] married', 'mutual', 'bilateral'). Strongest for romantic or personal pairs, weaker for other pairs (countries, teams).

Mixed. It fires on word pieces inside foreign or rare names and non-English or garbled text (Kh[[uras]]an, Sch[[les]]wig, Stojanovi[[ć]], Cyrillic/Greek fragments), and separately on 'of' in 'some of the' quantifier phrases plus a few other function words.

Fires on forms of the verb 'take' (take/taken/taking/takes/took) in phrasal or idiomatic uses: take advantage, take over, take up, take place, take effect, take steps. Other action verbs ('leave', 'earn', 'make') give weak to moderate activation.

Fires on middle word pieces of proper names, mostly foreign personal or place names (Alg[[ern]]on, Liebk[[ne]]cht, Kam[[al]], Safr[[an]]bolu, Sud[[bury]]), and of non-English words (Portuguese, Norwegian, German, Hungarian). The token is a sub-word fragment inside a multi-piece name or foreign word.

Fires mostly on 'the' or a word marking a measured outcome or quantity after verbs of improving, lowering or comparing (improving conversion rates and[[ the]] chances, bound on[[ the]] failure probability, enhance[[ the]] efficiency, 'median', '5-year' survival). Also fires on sentence-ending periods in results text. Activation is mostly moderate, apart from one strong top example.

Fires on the token that introduces a code block or example that follows: the colon in 'Here is my code:' or 'this script:', 'like' in 'something like this', 'this' in 'like this', 'example' in 'For example:', 'may refer[[ to]]:' on disambiguation pages, and closing code fences or indentation. Typical of Q&A and README text.
